topics.title: The Nurse-Advocate: Ethics, Autonomy & Social Justice
topics.summary: Advocacy means standing up for the client’s rights, values, and safety: protect a capable client’s choices, speak for a client who cannot, and fix unfair systems.
objectives: You can explain why advocacy is a duty under the ANA and ICN codes of ethics.
You can tell morals, ethics, and law apart and apply ethical principles.
You can name Bu and Jezewski’s three advocacy attributes and sort actions as micro or macro.
You can decide when to protect a client’s choice and when to speak for the client.
You can describe environmental quality as a health indicator (Exemplar 43.A).
topics.bigPicture:
Advocacy means supporting, defending, or helping another person’s cause. For a nurse, it means protecting the client’s rights, values, health, and safety. The ANA Code of Ethics (Provision 3) and the ICN Code of Ethics make this a duty, not a personality trait.

Advocacy is not giving clients whatever they ask for. It is also not deciding what is best and steering them there. You do one of three jobs. You protect the choices of a client who can decide. You speak for a client who cannot. You work to fix unfair systems. Knowing which job a moment calls for is the core skill here.
recap: Advocacy is an ethical duty (ANA Provision 3, ICN Code). It happens from the bedside to public policy.
Morals are personal. Ethics are professional codes. Law is enforced by society. At work, ethics and law guide you.
Three attributes: safeguard autonomy and act on behalf (microsocial); champion social justice (macrosocial).
A capable adult’s informed choice wins, even when the provider, the nurse, or the family disagrees.
Competence is a legal status. Capacity is a moment-to-moment ability that sedation or delirium can remove.
When you disagree, stay objective: inform, respect, and document. Show no approval or disapproval.
For a client who cannot decide, voice their known wishes and involve the legal decision-maker.
Ask the client privately who should help decide. Environmental hazards are a justice issue.

keyTerms.def: Supporting, defending, or helping another person’s cause. For nurses, protecting the client’s rights, health, and safety.
Acting for clients, families, groups, or communities so they get needed services and rights. Bu and Jezewski: actions that preserve, represent, or safeguard client rights, interests, and values.
First attribute (microsocial). Respecting a capable client’s right to make their own choices.

keyTerms.term: Acting on behalf of the client
keyTerms.def: Second attribute (microsocial). Representing the client’s values and rights when they cannot act or do not wish to.
Third attribute (macrosocial). Working in organizations, communities, and policy to remove health care disparities.
Your personal beliefs about right and wrong.
Formal standards for a profession, such as the ANA and ICN codes. They guide you even when your morals differ.
The client’s right to self-determination: making their own choices about their care.
Competence is a legal status set by a court. Capacity is the clinical ability, right now, to understand, weigh, and state a choice.
Deciding for a client “for their own good” and overriding their informed choice.
Choosing what the client would choose, based on known values. Used when wishes are known.
Choosing what would most benefit the client. Used when wishes are unknown, such as for a young child.
A culture where the family or group comes first, so decisions are often shared or made by an elder.
A health indicator showing how safe the air, water, soil, food, and housing are.

sections.heading: What is advocacy?
sections.keyIdea: Advocacy is a professional duty to protect the client’s rights, health, and safety.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, pp. 1, 3–4 (law row added)
sections.body:
Advocacy is supporting, defending, or helping another person’s cause. The ANA Code of Ethics, Provision 3, says the nurse promotes, advocates for, and protects the rights, health, and safety of the client. The ICN Code of Ethics says the same worldwide.

Patient advocacy has two classic definitions. The first: acting on behalf of others (clients, families, groups, or communities) to help them get services and rights they need but might not otherwise receive. The second, from Bu and Jezewski (2007): a series of specific actions that preserve, represent, or safeguard the client’s rights, best interests, and values in the health care system.

Nurses spend more direct time with clients than other providers, so they often notice problems first. You are ethically obligated to advocate for all clients. This is especially true for those unable to advocate for themselves. Examples are clients who are underserved, socioeconomically disadvantaged, or have poor health literacy. Advocacy can happen at one bedside or in a lawmaker’s office.

Keep three ideas apart: morals, ethics, and law. Morals are the principles you use to judge right and wrong from a personal point of view. Ethics are formal codes that govern professional conduct. When your morals clash with a client’s legal, informed choice, professional ethics win at work.

table.caption: Morals vs ethics vs law
rows: Personal. Never impose them on a client.
A binding duty when your morals and the client’s choice differ.
Enforced, such as consent and reporting laws. Breaking it brings legal or license penalties.

sections.heading: What are the three jobs of an advocate?
sections.keyIdea: Ask: can this client decide now, and is the problem one person’s or the system’s?
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, pp. 2–4
sections.body:
Bu and Jezewski (2007) described three core attributes of advocacy. Think of them as three jobs. The first two are microsocial, meaning they focus on one client. The third is macrosocial, meaning it focuses on organizations, communities, and policy.

The first two jobs do not conflict. They fit different moments. Before surgery, you protect the client’s own choices. During anesthesia, you voice the wishes the client already shared.

The third job rests on the ethics of justice. It aims to remove health care disparities, which are unfair gaps in care. It often starts with a bedside pattern. If many clients are readmitted because they cannot afford inhalers, that is a policy problem. Ways nurses do this third job:

table.caption: Bu and Jezewski’s three core attributes
rows: Client is competent and wants to take part

Encourages the client to share and document goals, preferences, values, and beliefs. Supports those values even if a provider disagrees. Gives enough timely facts at the client’s health literacy level.
Client cannot act or does not wish to (sedated, unconscious, advanced dementia, legally incompetent, a minor)

Monitors care quality and safety. Intervenes if care goes against the client’s wishes, directives, or best interests. Voices wishes during temporary incapacity, like anesthesia. Ensures a legal representative (power of attorney or guardian).
Helps clients reach goals by mobilizing agency and community resources. Acts at policy, organizational, local, state, and federal levels to remove disparities.

bullets: Mobilize agency and community resources for clients.
Work through groups like the ANA at state and national levels.
Speak in public or write for newspapers.
Lobby lawmakers or run for political office.
sections.analogy: With a capable client, you are a bodyguard for their choices. With a client who cannot speak, you are an interpreter of their known wishes. With a community, you are an organizer who changes the rules.

check.q: A nurse joins a committee to add evening clinic hours because low-income clients miss daytime visits. Which attribute?
check.a: Championing social justice, a macrosocial action that removes a system barrier.

sections.heading: How do you protect a capable client’s choice?
sections.keyIdea: A capable, informed client’s choice stands, even when others disagree.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, pp. 2–3 (capacity and principles table added for the NCLEX)
sections.body:
Autonomy is the client’s right to make their own choices. Safeguarding it assumes two things. The client holds the main responsibility for their own health and decisions. And the client is legally competent. The exceptions are a client who is not competent or who chooses not to be involved.

Competence is a legal status. Capacity is a clinical judgment made in the moment, by the provider with nursing input. Can the client understand, weigh the options, and state a choice? Sedation, delirium, or intoxication can remove capacity for a while.

A capable client may make an informed choice that conflicts with the provider’s advice or your own beliefs. Then stay objective. Mediate further discussion between the client and provider. Respect the client’s choice, and show no approval or disapproval. Objectivity keeps you from paternalism (deciding for the client) or coercion (pressuring the client until they agree).

Skilled advocates know they cannot act on every request. When a request cannot be met, explain why in plain language. Manage your own feelings about disappointing outcomes so they do not lead to frustration and burnout. The table links ethical principles to advocacy actions.

table.caption: Ethical principles behind advocacy
rows: Ask for a therapy that fits the client’s goals.
Stop a consent signing for a drowsy client.
Arrange an interpreter or a ride so access is equal.
Make the call you said you would make.
Give honest facts about risks and options.

sections.example: A client with a foot ulcer declines an amputation after the surgeon explains the risks. He correctly repeats that infection could spread and kill him. The nurse confirms he understands, documents the informed refusal, and tells the surgeon so they can discuss options. She does not say “That’s a mistake” or “Good for you.”

check.q: A capable client declines a flu shot. The nurse says, “I’d get it if I were you.” What is wrong?
check.a: It shows disapproval and pushes personal values. Confirm understanding, respect the choice, and document.

sections.heading: Speaking for a client who cannot decide
sections.keyIdea: Voice the client’s known wishes and involve the legal decision-maker.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, pp. 2–3, 5 (decision standards added for the NCLEX)
sections.body:
The second job applies when the client cannot act or does not want to speak for themselves. Examples are anesthesia, sedation, being unconscious, advanced dementia, legal incompetence, or being a minor.

Two standards guide decisions. Substituted judgment asks, “What would this client choose?” It is used when wishes are known. Best interest asks, “What would help this client most?” It is used when wishes are unknown.

You do not become the decision-maker. You watch care for safety and quality. You speak up if a treatment goes against the client’s wishes or advance directive. And you make sure the legal representative is involved, such as a durable power of attorney (health care agent) or a court-appointed guardian.
steps: Check whether the client can take part now, and whether a legal surrogate exists.
Find written wishes: advance directive, health care power of attorney, portable medical orders.
Tell the team those wishes, especially during anesthesia or sedation.
Watch the care given and speak up if it conflicts with the client’s wishes.
Escalate to the provider, charge nurse, or ethics committee if needed.
If no DPOA is on record for an incompetent client, contact the provider and social services.

check.q: A client’s advance directive refuses a breathing machine. During sedation, her oxygen drops and a resident prepares to intubate. What does the nurse do?
check.a: State the directive to the team right away and escalate to the attending provider. Other care she did not refuse continues.

sections.heading: Exemplar 43.A: Why does the environment matter?
sections.keyIdea: Environmental hazards harm health and cluster in poorer areas, so they are a justice issue.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, p. 1 (preview only); hazard details added — not in course materials
sections.body:
Environmental quality is a health indicator. It shows how safe the air, water, soil, food, and housing are. An environmental health hazard is an exposure there that harms health. Common hazards are listed below.

Hazards are not spread evenly. Low-income areas, rural homes with private wells, and places near industry carry more. So this is a justice issue. Teaching one family cannot fix a polluted water system.

At the bedside, take an environmental exposure history (the I PREPARE tool helps). Teach ways to lower risk, like carbon monoxide detectors. Refer for tests, such as blood lead screening. At the system level, report patterns to public health. Push for lead pipe replacement, clean air rules, and healthy housing codes.
bullets: Lead in old paint or pipes; pesticides; carbon monoxide.
Air pollution and secondhand smoke, which worsen asthma and heart disease.
Contaminated water, and mold or pests in poor housing.
Workplace exposures and extreme heat.
sections.example: A school nurse sees four children from one building with poorly controlled asthma. She finds mold and roaches in their homes. She teaches the families and refers the children to their providers (micro). Then she reports the building to the health department and housing authority (macro).

sections.heading: Who makes the decision in other cultures?
sections.keyIdea: Respect culture, but ask the client privately how they want decisions made.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, pp. 3–4
sections.body:
The idea that each client controls their own health choices is a Western view. In collectivist cultures, decisions are often shared. In the Hmong community, the head of the family, a community member, or a religious leader may decide. Illness may be seen as spiritual, not just physical.

Culture also shapes screening. In traditional Vietnamese culture, beliefs about who gets breast cancer affect the stage at diagnosis. So does the belief that a lump matters only if it hurts or is growing. In Appalachia, fatalistic beliefs (“what will be, will be”), low income, and access barriers lower HPV vaccine completion. Cervical cancer rates are higher there.

Your duty is to respect family and cultural traditions while honoring the client’s stated wishes and right to self-determination. Ask the client privately who should be involved. Use a qualified medical interpreter if needed. A client may choose to let an elder decide. That choice is itself autonomy. Never assume the family speaks for the client. Other helpful actions:
bullets: Explore beliefs first: “Tell me more about what you believe.”
Teach in plain, culturally tailored language.
Lower travel and cost barriers to care.
sections.example: A Hmong client with new cancer says, through an interpreter, that her eldest son and the clan leader should decide. The nurse documents this and sets up a family meeting with the interpreter. Later the son asks the nurse to hide the diagnosis. The nurse checks with the client about how much she wants to know.

check.q: A client says, “My husband decides about my health.” Does honoring this violate autonomy?
check.a: No. A capable client who freely hands off the decision is using her autonomy. Confirm it privately and document it.

sections.heading: Worked case: Donna Taylor and a drug interaction
sections.keyIdea: Validate the client’s fear, then ask the provider for an option that protects both her seizures and her mood.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, p. 8 (Clinical Example B)
sections.body:
Donna Taylor, 60, has major depressive disorder that is well controlled on an antidepressant. She has her first seizure. The ED physician orders an antiseizure drug that interacts with her antidepressant. He tells her, “You will need to discontinue your antidepressant so you can take this antiseizure medication.” Ms. Taylor is upset. She fears her depression will come back.

This case tests two skills. First, how you respond to her. Second, how you advocate with the physician. She is capable, so her voice counts in the plan. Your job is not to overrule the physician. It is to make sure her concern is heard and a safer option is explored.
steps: Recognize cues: a capable client, a stable mood on her current drug, and a plan to stop it suddenly.
Analyze: stopping a psychiatric drug abruptly risks withdrawal and relapse. Her fear is valid, not “noncompliance.”
Course question 1, nurse response: acknowledge her concern with empathy. Validate her right to take part in treatment decisions. Do not dismiss her fear.
Course question 2, advocacy with the physician: ask for an antiseizure drug that does not interact with her antidepressant.
Or ask for a consult with neurology, psychiatry, or a clinical pharmacist before her antidepressant is stopped abruptly.
Evaluate: the plan controls seizures, protects her mood, and she agrees with it.

check.q: Ms. Taylor says, “Maybe I just won’t take either pill.” What is the best nurse response?
check.a: “You’re worried about your depression coming back. Let’s talk with the doctor about options that treat the seizure without stopping your antidepressant.” Then notify the physician.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alike ideas
sections.keyIdea: Most traps turn on who decides and whether the client can decide now.
sections.source: Added: comparison table based on Module 43 study guide, pp. 2–3
sections.body: Two answers often both sound caring. Use this table to tell them apart.

rows: Advocacy supports the informed choice. Paternalism overrides it.
Can the client decide right now? Yes: protect the choice. No: voice their wishes.
The capable client’s own wish decides who is involved.
One client vs an organization, community, or policy.
Objective nurses stay involved and give facts. They just show no approval or disapproval.
Legal status vs clinical ability in the moment.
Explain limits plainly when a request cannot be met.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Pick the answer that respects a capable client and brings in the team.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials
sections.body:
Advocacy shows up as a client who refuses care or a family that wants to take over. Some items ask for the best response to a refusal. Others ask which action shows advocacy. Some ask whether an action is micro or macro. Wrong answers argue, promise outcomes, give in to family, or let the nurse decide.

Sample question: A 67-year-old client with end-stage kidney disease is alert and oriented. He decides to stop dialysis. His daughter says, “He’s depressed. Tell the doctor he doesn’t mean it.” Which action is most appropriate?

A. Tell the daughter the decision belongs to the client.
B. Explore his reasons and understanding, and notify the provider.
C. Encourage him to continue dialysis until the family agrees.
D. Request a psychiatric consult to declare him incompetent.
steps: Read the stem: an alert adult makes a choice; family disagrees and raises depression.
Really asking: the best action in an autonomy conflict.
Key cues: “alert and oriented” points to capacity. Depression is a cue to explore, not ignore.
A is wrong: true, but blunt. It skips checking his understanding.
C is wrong: it ties his right to family agreement. That is paternalism.
D is wrong: it assumes the result. Competence is a legal ruling.
Answer B: it assesses first and brings in the provider, who can judge capacity.
Strategy: pick the answer that checks understanding and involves the team.

sections.heading: Worked case: leaving against medical advice
sections.keyIdea: Success is an informed, supported choice, not whether the client stays.
sections.source: Added: worked example based on Module 43 study guide, pp. 2–3
sections.body:
Mrs. Alvarez, 81, is on IV antibiotics for pneumonia. She is alert, oriented, and stable. On day 2, she wants to leave. Her husband has dementia and is home with a neighbor who can only stay until morning.

Her son calls: “Don’t let her leave. She’s not thinking clearly.” The provider wants her to stay 48 more hours.
steps: Recognize cues: alert, oriented, stable. Her reason is a caregiving crisis, not confusion.
Analyze: this is safeguarding autonomy. The son cannot override her. But she needs full information about the risks.
Prioritize: confirm she understands the risks. Then address the real barrier, her husband’s care.
Generate solutions: tell the provider. Ask social work about respite or home health, and ask if oral antibiotics could allow safe discharge.
Take action: if she still leaves, the provider explains risks and she signs the against-advice form per policy. Give teaching and warning signs. Document objectively.
Evaluate: was her choice informed, and does she know when to return?

check.q: The son says, “If she leaves, I’m holding you responsible.” What should the nurse do?
check.a: Acknowledge his worry. Explain that his mother can make her own choices and the team is helping. Offer to include him, with her permission. Never restrain a capable client.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: NC law gives you the forms that put client wishes in writing.
sections.source: Added for NC practice — not in course materials (Disability Rights NC: study guide p. 4)
sections.body: NCLEX does not test state laws, but these facts shape NC practice.
bullets: The NC Board of Nursing (NCBON) regulates nursing under the Nursing Practice Act (G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.).
Under 21 NCAC 36 .0224, the RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment.
Health Care Power of Attorney (G.S. Chapter 32A, Article 3) names a health care agent.
Declaration of a Desire for a Natural Death (G.S. 90-321) is the NC living will.
The MOST form (Medical Orders for Scope of Treatment) is NC’s portable medical order. Ask about these documents and share copies.
Disability Rights North Carolina is the state’s federally mandated protection and advocacy agency for people with mental illness and disabilities.
NC is a Nurse Licensure Compact (multistate license) state. You follow the practice laws of the state where the client is located, including for telehealth.

sections.keyIdea: This lesson follows the Module 43 study guide; additions and name or date fixes are listed here.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, pp. 1–4, 8
bullets: Source: Module 43 study guide, pp. 1–4 (outcome 43.1, Exemplar 43.A preview, key terms, attributes, culture, public advocacy) and p. 8 (Example B).

Substituted judgment and best interest were added as standard ethics content.
