Patient advocacy (both definitions) and the full lists under each Bu and Jezewski attribute come from study guide pp. 1–3.
Each section names its exact pages, or says “Added” when it is not in the course materials.

mnemonics.name: SAC: the three advocacy jobs
mnemonics.text: S = Safeguard autonomy (the capable client decides). A = Act on behalf (the client cannot decide, so voice known wishes). C = Champion social justice (fix the system). S and A are micro; C is macro.

mnemonics.name: I PREPARE: environmental exposure history
mnemonics.text: Investigate potential exposures, Present work, Residence, Environmental concerns, Past work, Activities, Referrals and resources, Educate.

pearls: A capable adult’s informed decision rules, even when the provider, nurse, or family disagrees.
Family never overrides a capable client, unless the client freely chooses to let family decide.
Objective does not mean silent. Keep giving facts; just show no approval or disapproval.
Acting on behalf means voicing the client’s known wishes, not your own preferences.
The same problem in many clients calls for macrosocial advocacy.
If your morals block objectivity, ask for reassignment, but keep giving care until relieved.
redFlags: Family asks you to hide information from, or override, a capable client.
Pressure or threats used to get a client to agree to treatment.
A treatment about to start that goes against a written advance directive.
A client with poor health literacy or limited English making a major decision without a qualified interpreter or a plain-language explanation.
Several clients from one building with similar exposure illness, such as asthma or high lead levels.

checks.q: A nurse who opposes organ donation cares for a capable client who asks how to register as a donor. What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Give accurate information or connect the client with the donation resource, without disapproval. If the nurse cannot stay objective, ask another nurse to help.

checks.q: An unconscious trauma client carries a signed card refusing blood. The surgeon orders a transfusion. What is the first action?
checks.a: Tell the surgeon right away about the written refusal. This is acting on behalf of the client. Then escalate per policy.

checks.q: A nurse testifies before a county commission about the lack of buses to the only dialysis center. Microsocial or macrosocial?
checks.a: Macrosocial. This is championing social justice through local policy to remove an access barrier for a whole group.

checks.q: A Vietnamese client says she does not need a mammogram because her lump does not hurt. What is the advocacy response?
checks.a: Explore her beliefs. Explain, with an interpreter if needed, that painless lumps can be cancer. Help her get the visit, and respect her final choice.

checks.q: A parent in a pre-1978 rental asks why the nurse is asking about peeling paint. What is the nurse doing?
checks.a: Taking an environmental exposure history. Old lead paint is a major source of lead exposure in children.

checks.q: A client asks for an expensive brand-name drug that insurance will not cover. A generic equivalent exists. How does a balanced advocate respond?
checks.a: Explain plainly why the request may not be possible and explore the concern behind it. Ask the provider or pharmacist about alternatives or assistance programs. Do not promise what cannot be delivered.

topics.title: Advocacy Actions: Consent, Empowerment & Vulnerable Clients
topics.summary: Advocacy becomes action when you assess understanding and capacity, protect informed consent, build client skills, team up, and defend vulnerable clients’ rights.
objectives: You can do a rapid advocacy assessment, including capacity and reliability of the history.
You can check that consent is capable, informed, and voluntary, and act when a piece is missing.
You can name the legal surrogate and explain why the client’s nurse cannot be the surrogate.
You can choose empowerment tools and advocacy groups that fit the client.
You can protect the rights of children, people with disabilities, and other vulnerable groups.
topics.bigPicture:
Knowing you should advocate is easy. Knowing what to do in the next five minutes is harder. This lesson turns advocacy into actions. Find out what the client understands and whether they can decide. Make sure consent is real. Give them tools to manage their health. Bring in people who can help.

Informed consent is where advocacy is tested most. The provider gets consent. The nurse checks that the client can decide, has the facts, and is choosing freely. If any piece is missing, you stop and tell the provider. Vulnerable clients, like children and people with disabilities, need extra protection. Know their rights and who defends them.
recap: Assess first: understanding, health literacy, support, coping, capacity, and how reliable the history is.
Valid consent needs capacity, information, and free choice. If one is missing, stop and notify the provider.
The provider explains and obtains consent. The nurse verifies understanding and witnesses the signature.
Use a qualified medical interpreter for consent, never a family member or child.
A client without capacity needs a guardian or health care agent. The client’s nurse is never the surrogate.
No surrogate on record? Notify the provider and social services.
Empowerment builds skills and confidence. Confirm teaching with teach-back.
Psychiatric clients keep their rights, including refusing medication and freedom from non-emergency restraint.

keyTerms.def: A capable client’s free agreement after the provider explains the procedure, risks, benefits, and options, including no treatment.
A trained interpreter (in person, phone, or video). Family members and children should not interpret for consent.

keyTerms.term: Durable power of attorney for health care
keyTerms.def: A legal document in which a capable adult names an agent to make health decisions if they later lose capacity.
Federal law (1990, effective December 1991). Medicare and Medicaid facilities must tell clients their decision rights and advance directive policies, and document directives.
1990 civil rights law banning disability discrimination in jobs, schools, transportation, and public places. Amendments effective January 1, 2009, broadened who counts as disabled.
A partnership between client and providers, based on mutual commitment to patient-centered care (Palumbo, 2019). It replaces paternalism.
Five aspects of empowerment: self-efficacy, self-awareness, confidence, coping skills, and health literacy.
The client explains or shows, in their own words, what they learned. It is the best check of understanding.
Groups at higher risk of disease, disability, and early death due to lack of resources, risk factors, or both.
A person with both Medicare and Medicaid (12.2 million in 2018); among the sickest and poorest clients.
Protection and Advocacy for Individuals with Mental Illness. A federally mandated state agency that investigates abuse and protects rights (Disability Rights North Carolina).
National Alliance on Mental Illness. Local affiliates give support, education, and advocacy for people and families affected by mental illness.
Professionals reflecting on and building ways of practicing that give one integrated answer to client needs, through continuous interaction and knowledge sharing (IEC Expert Panel, 2011).

sections.heading: What does an advocate do, step by step?
sections.keyIdea: Assess first. You cannot protect wishes you have not heard.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, p. 6; example from p. 8 (Example B)
sections.body:
Advocacy follows the nursing process. Start with a rapid assessment. What does the client understand about the problem and the plan? What is their health literacy, support system, and coping? Next, can the client cooperate and decide? Is the history reliable, especially with memory or mental health problems? If not, involve family or the durable power of attorney (DPOA) as needed.

Then act. The steps list the core interventions.
steps: Rapid assessment: understanding, health literacy, support, coping.
Assess capacity and how reliable the history is.
Teach clients and families their legal rights in informed decision-making.
Make sure the client has an active voice in shared decisions with all providers.
Verify that enough information is given before informed consent.
Monitor care continuously, and evaluate agency policies that protect client rights.
Intervene if another provider disregards a competent client’s stated preferences or values.
sections.example: Donna Taylor, 60, has well-controlled depression and a first seizure. The ED physician orders a seizure drug that interacts with her antidepressant and tells her to stop it. She fears her depression will return. The nurse validates her concern. Then the nurse asks about a seizure drug without this interaction, or a specialist or pharmacist consult. Stopping a psychiatric drug abruptly risks withdrawal and relapse.

sections.heading: What makes consent valid?
sections.keyIdea: Consent counts only if the client has capacity, is informed, and chooses freely.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, p. 6 (watchdog scenario); consent elements and roles added for the NCLEX
sections.body:
Valid consent has three parts. The client has capacity. The client is informed about the procedure, risks, benefits, and options, including no treatment. And the client acts voluntarily, with no pressure.

The provider doing the procedure explains it and obtains consent. When the nurse witnesses the signature, it means the signature is the client’s and the client seemed capable and willing. It does not mean the nurse explained anything.

Your job is to verify. Stop if the client cannot explain the plan, has questions, is sedated, is pressured, or does not speak the form’s language. Tell the provider. Clients may withdraw consent any time. Use a qualified medical interpreter, never a family member or child. In a true emergency, when delay would threaten life or limb and no surrogate is available, implied consent allows treatment.

table.caption: Who does what in consent
rows: Verifies understanding, capacity, and free choice. Witnesses. Reports concerns. Documents.
Decides. May ask, refuse, or withdraw at any time.
Consents when the client lacks capacity.
Interprets accurately for limited English or hearing loss.

sections.example: This is the course’s “watchdog vs teamwork” scenario. A consulting physician comes for written consent from a client who got an opioid 20 minutes ago. The client is drowsy and cannot focus. The nurse acts as watchdog: she tells the physician the dose time and the client’s state. Then she acts as a teammate: together they decide to involve a designated family member, or to wait until the drug wears off. Then they repeat the talk, and the client re-signs. The nurse documents all facts objectively.

check.q: A client about to sign says, “I’m not sure what they’re removing, but the doctor is busy.” What does the nurse do?
check.a: Do not witness yet. Tell the surgeon the client needs more explanation, and document. The nurse does not explain the surgery in the surgeon’s place.

sections.heading: Which laws protect clients’ rights?
sections.keyIdea: The PSDA protects decision rights and advance directives. The ADA bans disability discrimination.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, p. 2 (course-vs-current date notes added)
sections.body:
Two federal laws come up often. The Patient Self-Determination Act (PSDA) requires health care institutions to tell clients their decision-making rights. They must also share their policies on advance directives. It gives general protection rights to all clients, including those with disabilities.

The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) is a civil rights law. It makes sure people with disabilities have the same rights as everyone else. It bans discrimination and gives federal protection in jobs, schools, transportation, and places open to the public.

Course vs current note. Your course guide says the PSDA was enacted in 1991. Current standard: Congress passed it in 1990, and it took effect December 1, 1991. The guide says the ADA was amended January 1, 2009. The ADA Amendments Act was signed in 2008 and took effect January 1, 2009. On a course exam, expect 1991 and 2009. The NCLEX does not test these dates.

table.caption: PSDA vs ADA
rows: Tell clients their decision rights and the facility’s advance directive policies
Equal rights for people with disabilities; bans discrimination
Health care institutions (in practice, those taking Medicare or Medicaid)
Jobs, schools, transportation, and public and private places open to the public
Ask about directives at admission and document them
Arrange interpreters, access, and reasonable accommodations

check.q: A Deaf client asks for a sign language interpreter for a clinic visit. Which law most directly supports this?
check.a: The ADA. It bans disability discrimination in places open to the public, including health care settings.

sections.heading: Who decides when the client cannot?
sections.keyIdea: A guardian or health care agent decides for a client without capacity. The client’s nurse never does.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, pp. 2, 5 (document table added for the NCLEX)
sections.body:
If a client lacks capacity, the legal guardian or the health care agent (durable power of attorney) gives consent. The nurse caring for the client may not be the surrogate. It is a conflict of interest with severe legal consequences.

No agent or guardian on record? Contact the provider and social services. They follow policy and state law to find the lawful surrogate. Never accept a signature from a friend or roommate.

Advance directives let clients plan ahead. The PSDA requires Medicare and Medicaid facilities to tell clients their rights at admission, ask about directives, and document them. Care cannot depend on whether a client has one.

Course vs current note. Your course guide says the nurse may NOT legally serve as the surrogate or DPOA. Current standard: the nurse caring for the client must never be that client’s surrogate.

Off duty, the law does not bar a nurse from being a health care agent for family or a friend. It is still a conflict best avoided. On a course exam, expect “the nurse may not serve as surrogate.” On the NCLEX, pick the same answer for any client in your care.

table.caption: Advance directives and related orders
rows: States which life-sustaining treatments the client wants or refuses. It applies only to the situations it names.
Durable power of attorney for health care
Names an agent who decides only when the client lacks capacity, using the client’s known wishes.
A court appoints a decision-maker after a finding of incompetence.
Provider-signed orders that travel with the client across settings. It is an order, not just a statement of wishes.
No CPR. It does not mean “do not treat.” Other care continues.

check.q: A client with advanced dementia needs a non-emergency procedure. No agent, guardian, or family is found. A roommate offers to sign. What does the nurse do?
check.a: Decline the roommate’s signature. Notify the provider and social services that no legal surrogate exists, and document.

sections.heading: How do you empower a client?
sections.keyIdea: Empowerment is a partnership that builds the client’s skills and confidence.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, pp. 2, 4 (teach-back added)
sections.body:
Empowerment replaces paternalism, where the provider decides and the client obeys. It is a partnership between client and providers, built on a shared commitment to patient-centered care (Palumbo, 2019). The client gains the knowledge and confidence to take part. Nurses are well placed for this because they spend more direct time with clients than other providers.

Nurses build self-responsibility, trust, and respect. They suggest safe support, like a hospital-run online cancer group rather than an open forum. Teach in plain language, in small chunks. Then confirm with teach-back.

The EMPATHIE framework names five aspects to build:
bullets: Self-efficacy: “I believe I can do this.”
Self-awareness: knowing my body, values, and triggers.
Confidence.
Coping skills.
Health literacy: finding, understanding, and using health information.

table.caption: Tools that support empowerment
rows: Disease self-management the client can reread. Match literacy and language.
Cell phone calls and text messages
Monitor care, support taking medicines, and offer guidance.
Real-time chronic disease self-monitoring and clinical review, like glucose or blood pressure logs.
Helps clients set self-care plans and health goals; helps rural clients.
Nurses build self-responsibility, mutual respect, trust, and confidence, and suggest safe support such as a hospital-run online cancer group.

check.q: A client with heart failure says, “I don’t get why I have to weigh myself.” What is the target, and how do you confirm success?
check.a: Health literacy. Explain that daily weight shows fluid gain. Then use teach-back: the client states when to weigh, what to report, and whom to call.

sections.heading: Who else can help the client?
sections.keyIdea: Advocacy often means getting the right person or agency involved.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, pp. 2, 4 (name corrections added)
sections.body:
Interprofessionality is how professionals reflect on and develop ways of practicing that give one integrated, cohesive answer to the client’s or population’s needs. It means continuous interaction and knowledge sharing between professionals to boost client participation (Interprofessional Education Collaborative Expert Panel, 2011).

Interprofessional collaboration increases shared decisions. It also links clients to emotional, teaching (instructional), and financial support. Get the pharmacist for drug interactions, the case manager for rides and home support, and the social worker for money or surrogate problems. Know the outside resources listed below.

Course vs current note. Your course guide calls these agencies “State Protection and Advisory Systems (PAIMI).” Current name: the Protection and Advocacy for Individuals with Mental Illness (PAIMI) program, run by each state’s protection and advocacy system. The guide also writes “Psychological Health Center for Excellence” and “Disability Rights of Ohio.” The correct names are Psychological Health Center of Excellence and Disability Rights Ohio. On a course exam, expect the guide’s wording. On the NCLEX, know what the agencies do.
bullets: NAMI (National Alliance on Mental Illness): hundreds of local affiliates and state organizations. They give support, education, awareness, and advocacy for people and families affected by mental illness.

PAIMI agencies: federally mandated nonprofit advocacy agencies. They investigate abuse and neglect and protect the rights of people with mental illness or disabilities. Examples: Disability Rights North Carolina, Disability Rights Ohio.

Military and veterans: deployed personnel are at high risk for PTSD. The Psychological Health Center of Excellence set baseline pre-deployment and post-deployment screening standards. The VA and DoD publish clinical guidelines for PTSD and acute stress reaction.

Professional and public advocacy: the ANA advocates at state and national levels. Nurses advocate alone or through associations by speaking in public, writing for the popular press, lobbying lawmakers, and running for office.
sections.example: A client with schizophrenia says group-home staff keep his money and cigarettes. The nurse tells her direct supervisor. She also gives him the number for Disability Rights North Carolina, the state PAIMI agency, which investigates abuse and protects his rights.

sections.heading: How do nurses advocate for children and families?
sections.keyIdea: Assess the family, mediate when needed, and change policies so children’s needs are met.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, pp. 4–5 (Table 43-1)
sections.body:
Children depend on adults to speak for them. Start by assessing the child and family. Then step in when things get complex. Nurses also act beyond the bedside, on committees and in the community. The bullets list these three actions.

Table 43-1 in the course lists community actions. The table below shows all three. Each one removes a barrier for many families at once, so it is macrosocial advocacy.
bullets: Assess the family’s needs, resources, and health literacy, and the child’s developmental level.
Mediate between family and provider when the family situation is complex or resources are limited. Intervene to prevent real or potential harm.
Serve on policy, practice guideline, and facility modernization committees. Make sure children’s developmental and psychosocial needs (play time, rest, nutrition) are met.

table.caption: Table 43-1: Community advocacy actions
rows: Compile a list of low-cost immunization and Vaccines for Children sites. Seek local grants to print and hand it out.
Collect travel-size hygiene donations. Arrange volunteer haircuts.
Partner with local newspapers and hand out posters about Safe Haven laws.

sections.example: A nurse sees low-income families skipping vaccines. She lists low-cost Vaccines for Children sites and gets a small local grant to print the list for clinics and churches.

check.q: A pediatric nurse joins a committee to keep the playroom open on weekends. Which course action is this, and what level?
check.a: It is like the course’s committee work for developmental needs (play, rest, nutrition). It is macrosocial, because it changes policy for all children on the unit.

sections.heading: How do you protect vulnerable clients?
sections.keyIdea: Vulnerable clients face more barriers and more harm, so watch for and defend their rights.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, pp. 2, 5 (violation examples added)
sections.body:
Vulnerable populations are groups at greater risk for disease, disability, and a shorter life. The cause is a lack of resources, risk factors, or both. They include underserved groups, low-income seniors, and younger people with physical or mental health disabilities. They also include people with limited English proficiency, dual-eligible clients, and research subjects. Key facts are listed below.

Clients in mental health settings keep their rights, listed in the table below (Disability Rights Ohio, 2020). Being in a facility does not remove basic U.S. citizenship rights, like voting, free speech, and freedom from unreasonable search. It also keeps the right to a safe living space, free from overmedication or excess restraint.
bullets: Dual-eligible clients have both Medicare and Medicaid (12.2 million people in 2018). They are the sickest and poorest clients, with higher rates of diabetes, lung disease, stroke, mental health disorders, and Alzheimer disease.
Research subjects with strict NIH advocacy protections: pregnant women, human fetuses and neonates (newborns), children, and prisoners.
Course disability statistics (ACLU, 2020): 70% of students secluded or physically restrained in public schools have disabilities.
60% of people in jail have a mental disability.
48% have a personal annual income of $15,000 or less.

table.caption: Rights of clients in mental health settings
rows: Safety with people they know (family, staff, strangers) and to be treated with dignity
To have or refuse a sexual relationship, including refusing another person’s touch
Not protecting a client from unwanted touch
To control money and possessions, such as cigarettes and clothing
Staff using a client’s money or taking his cigarettes
Treatment in a place that respects freedom, with a current written plan the client helped create
A plan written without the client
Freedom from drug or physical restraint, seclusion, or isolation except in an emergency
To refuse or accept suggested medication (no forced drugs except in an emergency)
To use rights without punishment, withheld treatment, lost privileges, or abuse
Losing phone time for refusing a dose

check.q: A calm psychiatric client refuses his evening antipsychotic. A technician says, “Then no phone calls tonight.” What does the nurse do?
check.a: Respect the refusal, notify the provider, and report the technician’s threat. Punishing a client for using a right is a violation.

sections.heading: How does advocacy link to other concepts?
sections.keyIdea: Each related concept has a link (why advocacy matters) and a nursing action (what you do).
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, pp. 6–7
sections.body:
Outcome 43.3 asks how advocacy connects to seven other concepts. For each one, learn two things. First, how it relates: advocacy raises or lowers something. Second, what the nurse does. The arrows in the course matrix mean “increases” or “decreases.”

A quick way to remember the set: cells, culture, ethics, systems, law, movement, and professionalism.

table.caption: Concepts related to advocacy (course matrix)
rows: More advocacy raises awareness of individual and global needs. It also raises funding for research and treatment.

Push for system and community changes that address discriminatory care and social disparities, like affordable healthy food. Push for cancer services (playtime, schooling, pet play areas) and research funding.
Advocating for cultural and religious preferences raises client satisfaction and strengthens the therapeutic relationship.
Give culturally competent care. Respect each client’s values, defend the right to such care, and promote equal care.
Ethics leads to advocacy. It raises client safety and autonomy.
Intervene when ethical dilemmas arise. Bring them to the provider, the team, and the ethics committee. Protect the right to choose and to refuse treatment.
Vulnerable clients face more access barriers, more challenges, and more discrimination.
Defend the right to access and equal care, especially in rural or underserved areas. Support telehealth and funding.
Advocacy raises client safety and autonomy, lowers the risk of negligence or error, and raises trust in nursing.
Uphold client rights in every situation. Monitor care by other professionals. Report unethical or illegal acts by any nurse, provider, or staff member.
Advocacy improves client and caregiver understanding, lowers the risk of more injury or immobility, and raises quality of life.
Push for access to care, the right devices (a walker sized for a short person), home safety checks, public accessibility, and research funding.
Acting professionally raises nurse credibility, so advocacy is more likely to succeed.
Advocate for clients at all times as part of your scope of practice. Act within professional and ethical standards.

check.q: A nurse reports a coworker who falsified a client’s vital signs. Which related concept fits best, and what does advocacy add?
check.a: Legal issues. Advocacy raises safety and trust in nursing and lowers the risk of negligence or error.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alike ideas
sections.keyIdea: Verify and escalate. Do not do the provider’s job, and do not do nothing.
sections.source: Added: comparison table based on Module 43 study guide, pp. 2, 4–6
sections.body: Use this table to separate answers that look alike.

rows: Provider explains; nurse verifies and witnesses.
Sedated, confused, pressured, or uninformed client: stop and tell the provider.
Never. Call the provider and social services.
Power of attorney for health care
One states wishes; the other names a person.
PAIMI investigates abuse; NAMI gives support and education.
PSDA: decision rights and directives. ADA: no disability discrimination.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: When any part of consent is missing, the first action is to stop and tell the provider.
sections.source: Added: worked example based on Module 43 study guide, p. 6
sections.body:
Expect consent scenarios with one missing piece, who may consent, rights violations, teach-back, and referrals.

Sample question: A client is scheduled for a cardiac catheterization. The consent is unsigned. He got IV morphine 15 minutes ago and is drowsy but wakes to voice. The cardiologist arrives with the form. What should the nurse do first?

A. Witness the signature because the procedure is scheduled.
B. Ask the spouse to sign the consent.
C. Tell the cardiologist about the morphine and the drowsiness.
D. Explain the procedure in simple terms.
steps: Read the stem: scheduled procedure, recent opioid, drowsy client.
Really asking: the first action when capacity is in doubt.
Key cues: morphine plus drowsiness; “scheduled” means there is time.
A is wrong: a sedated client cannot give valid consent.
B is wrong: the nurse does not pick a signer alone. Involving a designated family member or waiting is decided with the physician.
D is wrong: explaining is the physician’s job.
Answer C: the nurse informs the physician, and together they decide to wait or involve a designated family member, then repeat the talk.
Strategy: when any part of consent is missing, stop, tell the provider, and document.

sections.heading: Worked case: Lois Potter goes home on miglitol
sections.keyIdea: Do not let a ride rush an unsafe discharge. Check understanding first, then close the loop with the team.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, p. 8 (Clinical Example A); miglitol teaching added
sections.body:
Lois Potter, 78, has high blood pressure, heart disease, and new type 2 diabetes (a high A1C). The nurse practitioner prescribed miglitol, an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor. She already takes digoxin and amlodipine. The NP left for another consult. Mrs. Potter’s cab has arrived. The case management team meets later this morning.

The course asks two questions. What is the nurse’s first step? What should the nurse tell case management?
steps: Recognize cues: older adult, new drug, new diagnosis, a drug interaction, and a waiting cab.
Analyze: miglitol can lower digoxin bioavailability (how much digoxin gets into the blood). She may also not know how to take miglitol.
Course question 1, first step: assess her understanding of miglitol: timing with meals (first bite of each main meal), side effects (gas, loose stools), and the digoxin interaction.
Also arrange the ride or timing so she is not rushed out unsafely.
Course question 2, case management: report her discharge readiness, new diagnosis and drug needs, health literacy, and home support needs.
Make sure the NP, pharmacist, case manager, and nurse work together to verify medication reconciliation and follow-up.
Evaluate: she explains her plan with teach-back and has follow-up for digoxin and glucose.

check.q: The cab driver says he will leave in 5 minutes. What does the nurse do?
check.a: Ask the driver to wait or reschedule the ride. Safe teaching and medication review come before a convenient departure.

sections.heading: Worked case: consent and a language barrier
sections.keyIdea: Consent is not valid if a key risk was never explained.
sections.source: Added: worked example based on Module 43 study guide, pp. 5–6
sections.body: Mr. Reyes, 54, speaks Spanish and little English. He is set for a colonoscopy with possible polyp removal. His 15-year-old daughter has been interpreting. She tells the nurse, “He signed, but I didn’t know how to say ‘perforation,’ so I said it’s safe.” He is alert and has not been sedated.
steps: Recognize cues: limited English, a minor interpreting, a major risk not explained.
Analyze: consent is not valid. A child interpreter also risks errors and burdens her.
Prioritize: stop before the procedure. There is time to fix this.
Generate solutions: tell the physician; request a qualified medical interpreter; relieve the daughter.
Take action: the physician repeats the talk through the interpreter, and he re-signs if he agrees. Document the interpreter’s ID.
Evaluate: through the interpreter, he names bleeding and perforation as risks and chooses to proceed.

check.q: Which advocacy principles did the nurse use?
check.a: Informed consent (autonomy), equal access through an interpreter (justice), protecting a minor, teamwork with the provider, and objective documentation.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: NC law lets minors consent to some care and requires reporting disabled adults who need protection.
sections.source: Added for NC practice — not in course materials (Disability Rights NC: study guide p. 4)
sections.body: NCLEX does not test state laws, but these NC facts shape practice.
bullets: Minor consent (G.S. 90-21.5): minors may consent to care for sexually transmitted and other reportable diseases.
They may also consent to pregnancy care (not sterilization or abortion), substance or alcohol abuse care, and care for emotional disturbance.
Emancipated minors may consent. Adulthood begins at 18.
Advance directives: Health Care Power of Attorney (G.S. Chapter 32A, Article 3), living will (G.S. 90-321), and the MOST form. Ask about all three at admission and put copies in the record.
Disability Rights North Carolina is the state’s federally mandated protection and advocacy agency.
Disabled adults (G.S. 108A-102): anyone with reasonable cause to believe one needs protective services must report to the county DSS director, orally or in writing. Good-faith reporters are immune.
Under 21 NCAC 36 .0224, the RN delegates tasks, not judgment. Assessing capacity stays with the RN, not a Nurse Aide I or II.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.keyIdea: This lesson follows the Module 43 study guide; additions and name or date fixes are listed here.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, pp. 1–8
bullets: Source: Module 43 study guide, pp. 1–2 (outcomes 43.2–43.3, key terms), pp. 4–7 (empowerment, programs, children, vulnerable groups, consent rule, interventions, concept matrix), and p. 8 (Examples A and B). Cases and sample item are original.

PSDA: passed 1990, effective December 1, 1991 (the source says 1991). ADA Amendments Act: signed 2008, effective January 1, 2009 (the source says “amended January 1, 2009”). Both stated in “Which laws protect clients’ rights?”
The client’s own nurse must never be the surrogate. A nurse may be agent for family or friends personally, though the course advises against it.

States set a default surrogate order, applied by social services and the provider. For a client who is only briefly drowsy, the course has the nurse and physician decide together to wait or to involve a designated family member.
Miglitol teaching (first bite of main meals; GI effects; treat lows with glucose, not table sugar, if on insulin or a sulfonylurea) is standard pharmacology.

Correct names: Disability Rights Ohio (source: “Disability Rights of Ohio”); Psychological Health Center of Excellence (source: “for Excellence”); PAIMI is the Protection and Advocacy for Individuals with Mental Illness program (source: “State Protection and Advisory Systems”). Stated in “Who else can help the client?”
Nurse as surrogate: the source says the nurse may not legally serve as surrogate or DPOA. Current standard limits this to the client’s own nurse; stated in “Who decides when the client cannot?”
Concept matrix (pp. 6–7) is shown in full, with both the “relationship” and “nursing implications” columns. Table 43-1 is shown in full.
Lois Potter (Example A) is a worked case with both course questions answered.

mnemonics.name: CIV: three parts of valid consent
mnemonics.text: C = Capacity, I = Informed, V = Voluntary. Missing one? Stop and tell the provider.

mnemonics.name: EMPATHIE aspects: “Some Smart Clients Cope Literately”
mnemonics.text: Self-efficacy, Self-awareness, Confidence, Coping skills, health Literacy.

pearls: A drowsy client who just got an opioid cannot give valid consent for a non-emergency procedure.
Never use family, especially a child, to interpret consent.
The nurse caring for a client is never that client’s surrogate.
Restraint, seclusion, and forced medication are emergency-only, never punishment.
No agent or guardian for a client without capacity? Notify the provider and social services.
Teach-back is the best proof that teaching worked.
Check understanding before discharge, even when the ride is waiting.
redFlags: A client signing consent while sedated, confused, or saying they do not understand.
Restraint or seclusion used to punish or for staff convenience.
A psychiatric medication stopped abruptly with no plan or consult.
An incapacitated client with no legal surrogate facing a major decision.
A vulnerable client rushed out before teaching.

checks.q: A client says, “My son wants me to have this surgery, but I really don’t want it.” The consent is unsigned. What does the nurse do?
checks.a: Explore her feelings. Free choice is missing, so do not witness. Tell the surgeon she has said she does not want the surgery.

checks.q: A client with an intellectual disability has a court-appointed guardian and needs a dental extraction. Who consents, and what is the nurse’s role?
checks.a: The guardian consents. The nurse still explains in simple terms, seeks the client’s agreement, and shares his fears with the guardian and provider.

checks.q: A mother of an adult son newly diagnosed with schizophrenia wants to learn about the illness and meet other families. Which resource fits?
checks.a: A local NAMI affiliate. PAIMI agencies investigate abuse; they do not run family education.

checks.q: A client taught to use a glucose app says, “If my reading is over 300, I’ll wait until my visit in 3 months.” What does this show?
checks.a: A need for more teaching. The client should report high readings promptly per the plan.

checks.q: An older adult with Medicare and Medicaid, heart failure, and early Alzheimer disease is being discharged. Why does this client need extra advocacy?
checks.a: Dual-eligible clients are among the sickest and poorest. Assess understanding and capacity, involve the health care agent if needed, and have case management arrange medicines, follow-up, and home support.

topics.title: Reporting Unsafe Conduct: Impairment, Boundaries, Privacy
topics.summary: Nurses must stop and report unsafe, unethical, or unprofessional conduct by anyone on the team, starting with their direct supervisor.
objectives: You can explain the legal and ethical duty to report unsafe conduct, even by non-nurses.
You can use the chain of command, starting with your direct supervisor.
You can spot signs of impairment and act to protect clients.
You can tell a boundary crossing from a boundary violation.
You can respond to rights violations and social media privacy breaches.
You can sort practice events with Just Culture and report objectively.
topics.bigPicture:
The hardest advocacy moments are often with coworkers, not clients. Reporting a colleague who smells of alcohol can feel like betrayal. It is not. Your first loyalty is to client safety. State nurse practice acts and the ANA Code of Ethics both require you to step in and report unsafe or unethical conduct. This applies even when the person is not a nurse.

Reporting has a set order. First, protect the client from immediate harm. Then tell your direct supervisor, the person you report to. Some conduct also goes to the board of nursing or a protective agency. On the NCLEX, the right answer stops harm now and goes to the supervisor.
recap: Nurse practice acts and the ANA Code require you to report unsafe, unethical, substandard, or unprofessional conduct by anyone.
Stop the harm first. Then tell your direct supervisor. If the supervisor is the problem, go one level up.
Impairment can come from any substance or from extreme emotional distress. Report suspicion right away; proof is not needed.
Boundary violations, like romance with a client or coercive restraint, go to the supervisor and the board.
Any detail that could identify a client makes a post a privacy breach, even without a name.
Report facts, not labels. Chart client care; never mention the incident report in the chart.
Just Culture: console human error, coach at-risk behavior, discipline reckless behavior. Conduct issues go to the board.
Mandatory reports, like suspected child abuse, go straight to the legal agency. Telling a supervisor is not enough.

keyTerms.def: The legal and ethical duty to step in and report unsafe, unethical, substandard, or unprofessional conduct by any health care worker.
The facility’s reporting line. It starts with your direct supervisor and moves up if the issue is not fixed.
The person you report to, often the charge nurse or nurse manager. They give backup and help with reporting.
Being unable to practice safely due to legal, illegal, prescription, or over-the-counter substances, or extreme emotional distress.
Taking a client’s medication, often a controlled drug, for personal use or sale.
A brief departure from usual limits that helps the client, like a short self-disclosure, then returns to normal.
Conduct that serves the staff member and harms or exploits the client, such as a romance or coercive restraint.
Sharing protected client information, such as health facts, talk, or photos, whether on purpose or not.
A quality and risk tool for unusual events. It is not part of the chart.
A fairness model that judges the nurse’s choice, not the outcome. It separates human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless behavior.
A board program that lets a nurse with a substance use disorder get treatment and monitoring instead of standard discipline.
A federally mandated state agency (Disability Rights North Carolina) that investigates abuse of people with mental illness or disabilities.

sections.heading: Why report, and who do you tell first?
sections.keyIdea: Stop the harm, then tell your direct supervisor. The duty covers anyone on the team.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, p. 7 (steps and reporting table added for the NCLEX)
sections.body:
Reporting is advocacy at two levels. It protects the client in front of you (microsocial). It also fixes the system so the next client is safe (macrosocial).

The duty comes from two places: your state nurse practice act and the ANA Code of Ethics. Both require you to intervene and report. The duty is broad. It covers unethical, unsafe, substandard, and unprofessional conduct. It applies to nurses, providers, technicians, aides, students, and other staff. Staying silent when a client is at risk can lead to discipline for you.

Follow your facility’s procedure. The first report goes to your direct supervisor, the person you report to directly. The supervisor helps you report and gives immediate backup to protect the client. If the supervisor is involved or does nothing, go up the chain. Some conduct must also go to outside agencies.
steps: Protect the client now. Stop the unsafe act if you safely can, and assess the client.
Tell your direct supervisor right away, in private, with facts.
Let the supervisor relieve the person from care. Do not leave clients alone.
Document client-care facts and who you notified. Complete an incident report per policy.
Go up the chain if the issue is not fixed or the supervisor is involved.
Report to outside agencies when required, usually with supervisor and risk management support.
bullets: When you report or document, state what you saw: “slurred speech, alcohol odor at 0705.”
Avoid labels like “she is obviously an alcoholic.”
Never write “incident report filed” in the client’s chart.

table.caption: Who to tell
rows: Board of nursing per policy and law
Staff restrains or coerces a client
Board and protection and advocacy agency
Charge nurse, then up the chain
Supervisor per policy, but never instead

sections.analogy: Reporting is like pulling a fire alarm. You are not accusing anyone. You are getting trained help before someone is hurt.

check.q: A new nurse believes her charge nurse is impaired. Whom does she tell?
check.a: The next level up, such as the nurse manager or house supervisor. When the supervisor is the problem, skip to the next level.

sections.heading: How do you spot an impaired coworker?
sections.keyIdea: Suspicion is enough. Report right away; do not investigate on your own.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, p. 7 (signs table added for the NCLEX)
sections.body:
Impairment can come from legal, illegal, prescription, or over-the-counter substances. It can also come from extreme emotional distress, like returning to work right after a close family member’s death. The ANA (2015a) says any nurse who sees or suspects impairment in any health worker must report it to a supervisor immediately.

You do not need proof. Do not search lockers or watch for hours to “be sure.” Substance problems often show as practice patterns first. Many impaired nurses are skilled and well liked, so coworkers explain away the signs. Reporting often gets the colleague help through an alternative-to-discipline program.

table.caption: Signs of possible impairment
rows: Mood swings, frequent absences, long breaks, asking for clients on opioids
Slurred speech, alcohol odor, unsteady gait, pinpoint or dilated pupils, drowsiness
Wastes without a witness, count errors, clients with unrelieved pain after doses
Crying, poor focus, errors after a recent loss

check.q: A nurse returns two days after her father’s sudden death. She has made two medication errors and is crying. What should a coworker do first?
check.a: Notify the supervisor, such as the charge nurse, right away so her clients are covered and she can be relieved. Grief can impair practice just as substances can. Respond with compassion.

sections.heading: Where is the line with boundaries?
sections.keyIdea: Ask whose need is being met. The nurse, not the client, keeps the boundary.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, pp. 3, 7 (crossing vs violation added for the NCLEX)
sections.body:
The therapeutic relationship exists to meet the client’s needs. The nurse holds the power, so the nurse keeps the boundary, even if the client starts it.

A boundary violation is unethical or unsafe conduct that crosses professional limits. It serves the staff member and harms or exploits the client. Examples are an inappropriate relationship with a client and coercing or restraining a client to benefit staff. Dating, money deals, and secrets also count. You must intervene and report violations to your supervisor and the state board of nursing.

A boundary crossing is different. It is brief, helps the client, and returns to normal.

Boundaries also apply in your personal life. Do not act as a friend’s clinician or surrogate. See the Heather Adams case below.

table.caption: Crossing or violation?
rows: Briefly sharing your own knee surgery to ease a client’s fear
Planning coffee with a client after discharge
Restraining a client who refused to share with staff

check.q: A client says, “You’re the only one who understands me. Can we keep in touch after I go home?” Best response?
check.a: Acknowledge the bond, explain the relationship is professional and ends at discharge, and connect the client with ongoing support.

sections.heading: Worked case: William Johnson was restrained
sections.keyIdea: Believe the report enough to act, and report it up and out.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, p. 8 (Clinical Example C); action steps added
sections.body:
William Johnson, 53, has COPD and schizophrenia. At his clinic visit, he says a psychiatric technician restrained him in bed during his last admission. Why? He refused to share his cigarettes with the technician.

Several of his rights were violated, and it is a severe boundary violation. The table gives the course answers. Advocacy here is both micro (his safety) and macro (stopping abuse in the facility).

His diagnosis does not make the report less believable. People with mental illness face a higher risk of abuse.
steps: Listen without judging. Thank him and assess his current safety.
Document his words objectively, with date and time.
Report to your supervisor or facility administration right away.
Make sure reports reach protective and licensing agencies, like Disability Rights North Carolina.
Tell him his rights and resources he can contact himself.
Follow up and support policy changes, like staff training.

table.caption: Course questions and answers
rows: Control of personal possessions (his cigarettes). Freedom from physical restraint except in an emergency. Freedom from abuse and coercion. It is also a severe boundary violation and unethical staff conduct.
Report right away to the direct supervisor or facility administration. Make sure it reaches protective agencies (the state PAIMI or Disability Rights agency) and the state licensing board.
What level of advocacy is this?
Both. Microsocial: protecting his own safety and rights. Macrosocial: reporting abuse in the facility so policy changes.

sections.heading: What can you post on social media?
sections.keyIdea: If any detail could identify a client, do not post it. Removing the name is not enough.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, p. 7 (post examples added for the NCLEX)
sections.body:
Posting confidential client information breaches privacy laws such as HIPAA. This includes health facts, conversations, and photos. It is a breach whether done on purpose or without meaning harm. A room number, rare condition, date, or location can identify someone. Private groups and deleted posts still count.

Penalties include employer and board discipline, plus civil and criminal penalties (NCSBN, 2018). Nurses must monitor colleagues and report breaches right away. Do not friend clients or talk about them negatively online, even without names.

table.caption: Safe or violation?
rows: “Proud of my team tonight!” with no client details
Unit selfie with a client’s wristband in view
Rare tumor described in a private nurses’ group
“Guess which famous athlete is in Room 4!”
Sharing a public health vaccine post

check.q: A coworker posts a client’s X-ray captioned “Look what we pulled out today!” No name shows. What should the nurse do?
check.a: Treat it as a privacy breach and report it right away to the supervisor or privacy officer. Do not share or comment on it.

sections.heading: How does Just Culture sort mistakes?
sections.keyIdea: Judge the choice the nurse made, not the outcome. Conduct issues go to the board.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials
sections.body:
Many employers and boards use a Just Culture approach. It asks, “What choice did the nurse make?” Two nurses can make the same error, one with harm and one without. The response should match the behavior, not luck. Repeated at-risk behavior after coaching moves toward reckless.

Conduct issues are not errors to coach away. They include diversion, impairment on duty, fraud, boundary or sexual misconduct, and confidentiality breaches. These go to the board, not just the employer.

A fair system makes honest reporting more likely. Nurses who fear punishment hide errors, and hidden errors repeat. Advocacy includes reporting your own errors promptly.

table.caption: Just Culture at a glance
rows: Sets a pump at 100 instead of 10 mL/h after an interruption
Console the nurse; fix the system
A chosen shortcut; risk not seen or rationalized
Coach; remove the pressure to cut corners
Knowing disregard of a big risk
Gives a high-alert drug with no order after a warning
Discipline; may be reported to the board
Diversion, impairment, fraud, sexual misconduct, privacy breach
Report to the board of nursing; alternative-to-discipline may apply for substance use

check.q: A nurse gives metoprolol to the wrong client. Two clients with similar names were moved next door to each other, and the scanner has been broken for a week. She reports it at once. How is this classified?
check.a: Human error made likely by the system. Console her, monitor the client, notify the provider, file an incident report, and fix the scanner and name alerts.

sections.heading: Worked case: Heather Adams asks you to decide
sections.keyIdea: Stay a friend, not her nurse or proxy. Send her to an attorney to name a trusted non-nurse.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, p. 9 (Reflect Case)
sections.body:
Heather Adams, 31, is your unmarried neighbor. She has a history of depression. Her mother has Alzheimer disease. Her only brother is her legal next of kin, but they are estranged. If she becomes incapacitated, she does not want him making her medical decisions. She asks you, a nurse, for help.

Course vs current note. Your course guide says a nurse should not be her surrogate because it is an ethical conflict of interest. Current standard: no law bars a nurse from being a friend’s health care agent. The conflict is real if you are also her clinician. On a course exam, expect “No, the nurse should not be her surrogate.” On the NCLEX, the safe answer is the same: keep roles separate and refer to legal help.

table.caption: Course questions and answers
rows: A supportive neighbor and friend, not her assigned clinical nurse. Do not blur personal and professional boundaries.
No. Per the course, a nurse serving as her health care proxy or DPOA creates an ethical conflict of interest.
Strongly encourage her to see an attorney. She can sign a durable power of attorney for health care (health care proxy) and a living will naming a trusted friend or non-nurse advocate.

check.q: Heather asks, “Can’t you just tell the hospital what I want if something happens?” Best reply?
check.a: “I care about you, and I want your wishes to be legal and clear. An attorney can help you name someone in a health care power of attorney and write a living will.”

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alike ideas
sections.keyIdea: Reporting questions turn on order (who first) and target (who gets the report).
sections.source: Added: comparison table based on Module 43 study guide, pp. 3, 5, 7
sections.body: Use this table to separate answers that look alike.

rows: The supervisor is the first report.
Board reports follow the supervisor. Exception: child abuse goes straight to DSS.
Crossing helps the client; violation serves the nurse.
Emergency means imminent danger; coercion means punishment or staff benefit.
Covering for impairment endangers clients and the coworker.
At-risk: risk not seen (coach). Reckless: risk known and ignored (discipline).

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: The first action stops the harm and goes to the direct supervisor.
sections.source: Added: worked example based on Module 43 study guide, p. 7
sections.body:
Expect questions on first action with an impaired coworker, whom to tell, boundary behaviors, social media posts, and rights violations.

Sample question: On night shift, a nurse sees a colleague with slurred speech and alcohol odor about to give IV morphine to a postoperative client. Which action should the nurse take first?

A. Tell the colleague to go home and offer to cover her clients.
B. Ask the colleague to hand over the morphine and notify the charge nurse now.
C. Report the colleague to the state board of nursing.
D. Write an incident report before the end of the shift.
steps: Read the stem: signs of impairment, and a high-risk drug about to be given.
Really asking: the first action when harm is about to happen.
Key cues: “about to give IV morphine” means harm is imminent. Suspicion is enough.
A is wrong: sending her home is the supervisor’s call, and she may drive impaired.
C is wrong: the board may come later, but it does not protect this client now.
D is wrong: documenting is needed but does not stop the dose.
Answer B: it stops the harm and tells the direct supervisor.
Strategy: stop the harm, tell the supervisor, then document and report outside.

sections.heading: Worked case: a pattern in the drug records
sections.keyIdea: Patterns plus physical signs call for a prompt, private, factual report.
sections.source: Added: worked example based on Module 43 study guide, p. 7
sections.body: Jordan, an RN, notices that a well-liked colleague, Sam, often signs out hydromorphone for clients with pain scores of 2 out of 10. Sam asks others to cosign wastes later and takes long breaks. Two of Sam’s clients say their pain was not relieved. Today Sam is drowsy with pinpoint pupils and has four postop clients.
steps: Recognize cues: practice signs plus drowsiness and pinpoint pupils suggest diversion and impairment.
Analyze: clients are at risk now. Diversion is a conduct issue, not a simple error.
Prioritize: today’s safety first. Sam’s clients need a safe nurse and pain reassessment.
Generate solutions: who must know now, what Jordan must refuse to sign, and which clients need reassessment.
Take action: privately tell the charge nurse or manager the facts now. Refuse to cosign wastes you did not see. Reassess clients in pain.
Follow through with the supervisor: relieve Sam, follow policy (testing, pharmacy audit), and report to the board as required.
Evaluate: clients are safe, facts are documented, and Jordan seeks support.

check.q: Sam says, “Please don’t tell anyone. I’ll get help on my own.” What should Jordan do?
check.a: Show care, but explain that client safety requires reporting. Then tell the supervisor. Keeping the secret is covering up. Reporting often leads to an alternative-to-discipline program.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: In NC, conduct issues go to the Board, and anyone who suspects child abuse must report to DSS.
sections.source: Added for NC practice — not in course materials
sections.body: NCLEX does not test state laws, but these facts shape NC practice.
bullets: The NC Board of Nursing (NCBON) regulates nursing under the Nursing Practice Act (G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.).
NCBON uses a Just Culture–based Complaint Evaluation Tool: human error, at-risk behavior, or reckless behavior.
Conduct issues (diversion, impairment on duty, fraud, boundary or sexual misconduct, confidentiality breaches) are reported to the Board.
NCBON offers alternative-to-discipline programs for substance use.

Child maltreatment (G.S. 7B-301): NC is a universal reporting state. Anyone who suspects abuse, neglect, or dependency of a child under 18, or a death from maltreatment, must report to the county DSS director, orally or in writing. Good-faith reporters are immune.
Report suspicion; do not wait for proof. Knowingly failing to report is a crime.
Disabled adults (G.S. 108A-102): anyone with reasonable cause to believe one needs protective services must report to the county DSS director.
NC is a Nurse Licensure Compact state. Follow the laws where the client is; discipline can affect your multistate privilege.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.keyIdea: This lesson follows the Module 43 study guide; additions and clarifications are listed here.
sections.source: Module 43 study guide, pp. 1, 3, 7–9
bullets: Source: Module 43 study guide, p. 1 (43.4), p. 3 (boundary violations), p. 7 (duty to report, chain of command, impairment, social media), p. 8 (Example C), p. 9 (Heather Adams). Cases and sample item are original.
“Supervisor first” applies to workplace conduct. If harm is imminent, stop the harm first.
Legally required reports (child abuse; disabled adults) go to the agency from the person who suspects. Telling a supervisor does not meet that duty.
Boundary crossing vs violation and NCSBN social media rules were added as standard content.

Heather Adams: the source says a nurse serving as her proxy is an ethical conflict. A nurse is not legally barred from being a friend’s agent; the conflict is strongest if the nurse is her clinician. Stated in “Worked case: Heather Adams asks you to decide.” The advice is the same.
Just Culture is not in the study guide. It was added because it is tested and NCBON uses it.
Duty to report comes from both the state nurse practice act and the ANA Code (p. 7). The direct supervisor’s role (helps report, gives immediate backup) is from p. 7.
William Johnson (Example C) now lists all three course questions and answers.

mnemonics.name: STOP-TELL-WRITE
mnemonics.text: STOP the harm. TELL your direct supervisor (next level if the supervisor is involved). WRITE objective facts. Outside reports follow policy and law.

mnemonics.name: Crossing vs violation: “Whose need is met?”
mnemonics.text: Client’s need, brief, returns to normal = crossing. Nurse’s need, secret, repeated = violation.

pearls: The duty to report covers everyone on the team, not only nurses.
Suspicion of impairment is enough. Do not wait for proof or investigate.
The first report goes to your direct supervisor. Go higher if the supervisor is involved or does nothing.
Protect the client first when harm is imminent.
A psychiatric diagnosis never makes an abuse report less credible.
Removing a name does not make a client post safe.
The nurse, not the client, is responsible for keeping professional boundaries.
redFlags: A coworker with signs of intoxication about to give medications.
Count errors, late waste cosigns, or clients with unrelieved pain after doses.
Restraint or threats used to punish or benefit staff.
A staff member keeping secrets with, dating, or trading money with a client.
Client photos or details posted online by any staff member.

checks.q: A nurse sees an aide tying a confused client to a chair with a sheet “just until my break is over.” What does the nurse do first?
checks.a: Remove the sheet, stay with the client, and assess for injury. Then report to the charge nurse. Protect the client before reporting.

checks.q: A surgeon skips the surgical time-out even though the circulating nurse asks for it. What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Speak up right away to stop the procedure until the time-out is done. Then report through the chain of command, such as the perioperative manager, with objective documentation.

checks.q: A nurse in NC sees a 3-year-old with glove-like burns on both hands. The story does not fit. What is the priority?
checks.a: Report suspected abuse to the county DSS. Do not wait for test results or let the charge nurse decide; the duty is the nurse’s own.

checks.q: A nurse skips barcode scanning, saying “It’s faster, and I check the label.” No harm occurred. How does Just Culture classify this?
checks.a: At-risk behavior. The response is coaching on the risk and removing pressures that reward the shortcut.

checks.q: A charge nurse tells a staff nurse to ignore a colleague’s intoxication because the unit is short. What should the staff nurse do?
checks.a: Go to the next level, such as the house supervisor, right away. Short staffing never justifies an impaired nurse giving care.
